04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma opened Fiona's email before breakfast. The records team had finally examined the first sheet inside the folder marked “Payment exceptions — 2011”. It was a guide to the words used in the trust's accounts, not a list of students.

The guide described three reasons for marking a payment as an exception: missing documents, a changed travel plan, or a payment returned by the bank. It did not say how often these things had happened. Fiona warned Emma that the team had not checked the individual records.

“Does a returned payment mean a student lost their grant?” Emma asked.

“Not necessarily,” Fiona said. “The money might have been sent again after the problem was fixed. We don't know.”

Emma called Sarah. They had spent weeks trying to understand why selected students and payments might not match. Now they had a possible explanation, but no figures.

“So the foundation did have problems with payments,” Sarah said.

“It had a way to record problems,” Emma corrected her. “That's different from proving any particular payment failed.”

They made a list of the evidence they still needed: how many exceptions had been recorded, what happened afterwards, and whether any transfer had finally reached a student.

Later Helen Ward replied to Emma's question about her cousin's grant. Her cousin had found no bank statement from 2011 and did not remember the exact date of any payment. Helen asked Emma not to treat this as proof that the money had never arrived.

Emma agreed. An old statement might have been lost. A forgotten date was not a missing payment.

In the afternoon Fiona sent one more detail. The guide told staff to write a second reference beside any exception that had been resolved. Fiona did not yet know whether the surviving records included those second references.

“Then we should ask for totals of open and resolved cases,” Sarah suggested.

“Yes, if the records allow a reliable count,” Emma said.

Emma remembered the anonymous caller's warning about the people who signed the payments. She still could not identify the caller, and she refused to assume the warning was true.

Before closing her notebook, she drew two columns: Exception recorded and Exception resolved. Between them she left a space for documents she had not seen.

Then a new email arrived from Fiona. The records team had noticed that some entries used the words “manual approval”. Fiona had not checked who approved them or what they were for.

Emma stared at the phrase. It might describe an ordinary office task. But now she knew exactly which question to ask next.
